Wiktor Tomasik — Strange loop in J-space

Research in The Mind in the Mirror: Self-Models at https://pixedar.github.io/.

A small trainable reader summarizes a frozen language model's internal activity. The numerical summary sets an eight-dimensional control state, which changes the next reading. Training asks the summary to distinguish the loop's possible updates after subtracting their common destination. This centered-field objective removes the shortcut of identifying a copy by one destination.

In an initial small-model comparison, 2 of 5 self-description runs sustained substantial state dependence without persistent two-state oscillation. Three additional runs from previously trained interfaces reached the criterion during training. Samples are small and share starting interfaces. Controls describing another run's recordings remain close to a common destination. The interactive comparison displays all 12 starting-state responses at 60 text positions and four copies using distances in the full eight-dimensional space.

In the strongest developmental run, holding the reader's state input fixed reduces large steps from 26.6% to 1.2%; holding the route into the language model fixed leaves 26.4%. Applying the reader's attention inside the model changes its highest-probability next token at 11–16% of positions across five self-description runs. Prediction-loss changes are mixed, and the control also changes predictions. Feedback through model processing contributes little to the measured state dependence.

The strongest run's normalized dependence score is 0.65 versus 0.002 for the control. It is a ratio of squared variations, not a causal percentage. Predicted and measured patterns correlate at +0.81, but predictions have large scale errors. Copies can converge on shared text. Stable personality, a representation of the effects of attention, and subjective experience are not established.

Separate experiments study word-based J-space feedback, casual-persona drift, invented conversational history, a rotating time code across reasoning segments, controlled evidence selection, and text/image/audio inputs. Their mechanisms and limits are documented separately.

Author: Wiktor Tomasik
